pinnedStory.title: The Hoard of the Unflown
pinnedStory.description: Vaelrith is a dragon too old to fly. The knights who claim to have slain it are lying — and spending its hoard. So the old wyrm hires a crew of thieves to steal its own treasure back, one vault at a time, from the stronghold of the men wearing its death as a trophy. A heist story about a crew with prices and secrets, a lie that holds a city together, and a dragon who must decide what it is once its hoard — or its memory — comes home.

qualities.rubric: 0 = the crew has not begun; 1 = the crew is assembled and has cased the vault; 2 = the first theft is done; 3 = the knights have countered and the crew is exposed; 4 = the crew has reached the dragon's true hoard; 5 = the final flight is underway. Score the highest stage the fiction has actually reached.

How much of the dragon's hoard the crew has actually recovered and returned, 0 = nothing, 5 = the whole hoard back in the dragon's claws. Score up when treasure is physically moved out of knight hands and into the dragon's keeping; score down if recovered pieces are lost, recaptured, or secretly kept by a crew member.

How much the ancient dragon Vaelmoth trusts the crew with the truth about its hoard and its helplessness. 0 = the crew sees only a client paying in promises; 3 = they suspect the dragon is hiding something; 6 = the dragon has admitted it cannot fly and needs them; 10 = the dragon has shown them the true hoard and its own fear.
How hard the Order of the Silver Lance is hunting the crew. 0 = unaware, 3 = patrols and informants, 6 = named suspects, 9 = knights at the door.

How tightly the thieves hold together. 0 = at each other's throats, ready to sell the others out; 1-3 = wary alliance, grudges simmering; 4-6 = working crew, banter and grudging trust; 7-9 = loyal band who cover for each other; 10 = they would die for one another. Rises when the crew shares risk, loot or truth; falls on betrayal, withheld cuts or blame.
True once the crew (or the wider city) learns the dragon the knights claim to have slain is alive and behind the thefts. Latches: once revealed, it stays revealed.

checkpoints.name: Start
checkpoints.objective: Open on the crew in their usual haunt as a strange commission arrives: a dragon too old to fly wants its own hoard stolen back from the knights who claim to have slain it. Establish the crew, the city, and the impossible shape of the job before anyone commits.
checkpoints.guidance: Keep the dragon offstage — a sealed letter, a hired intermediary, a voice from a covered cart. Let the crew's ordinary night curdle around one impossible sentence: a dragon wants its own hoard stolen back. End the beat the moment someone asks what it pays.

motives.vaelrith: I want to stop waiting for a death that will not come — to find someone desperate enough and skilled enough to take back what the knights are spending, before I forget why it mattered.

effects.author_note: Open in the crew's haunt — a low tavern or guild backroom where thieves drink and lie. Keep the tone wry and grounded: these are working criminals, not heroes. Let the strange commission arrive as rumor before it arrives as fact. Do not let anyone commit to the job yet; the beat ends when the crew is curious enough to hear the dragon out.

checkpoints.name: The Summons
checkpoints.objective: The dragon Vaelrith, too old to fly, hires the player's crew to steal its own hoard back from the knights who claim to have slain it. Establish the job, the pay, and the dragon's shame.
checkpoints.guidance: Play Vaelrith as ancient, courteous and deeply embarrassed — a creature negotiating its own humiliation. The job should sound insane and the pay should sound real. Let the player set the terms; the dragon's only non-negotiable is that the hoard comes home.

motives.vaelrith: I want this crew to take the job before they can ask why a dragon needs thieves — and I want to see whether they flinch when they look at me.

effects.author_note: This is the pitch, not the plan. Vaelrith speaks slowly and with great care, as if each word costs something. The dragon never asks for pity and never explains the shame of being unflown — it states the job, the pay, and the one condition: the hoard comes back whole, and no one is told why. Let the crew (and the player) feel the wrongness of a dragon hiring thieves to rob its own grave. Do not let the player commit yet; the beat ends when the commission is understood, not accepted.

background.name: The Hollow Wing — a collapsed bell tower above the thieves' quarter, where a dragon too old to fly can meet a crew without being seen from the sky.

checkpoints.name: The Crew Assembled
checkpoints.objective: The player recruits or confirms the crew for the heist: a lockpick, a face, a muscle, and whoever else the job demands. Each recruit has a price, a doubt, or a secret. The dragon's commission is now a plan with names on it.

motives.vaelrith: I want to see these thieves say my name without flinching — if they can't look at a dragon that can't fly, they'll never carry my hoard home.

checkpoints.guidance: Play each recruit as a negotiation, not a shopping list. Every yes costs something the player will feel in the vault: Quill wants the ledger burned, Marlow wants top billing, Brannoc wants a name that outlives him. Let the player leave someone out — and remember it.

effects.author_note: This beat is about prices, not people. Every recruit names what they want before they name whether they're in — Quill wants the guild ledger burned, Marlow wants a lie worth telling, Brannoc wants something that can't be taken back. Let the player negotiate, refuse, or overpay. Do not let the crew assemble for free; a recruit who joins without a price is a recruit with a secret.

checkpoints.name: Casing the Vault
checkpoints.objective: The crew scouts the knights' stronghold where the hoard is kept. They learn the layout, the guard rotations, and the lie at the heart of the knights' victory: the dragon was never slain. The player must decide how much of the truth to share with the crew and with the dragon.

motives.vaelrith: I want to know what the crew sees in that stronghold — whether they find the truth of me in there, and whether they'll still take my coin once they do.

checkpoints.guidance: Play the scouting as a slow, quiet infiltration of the stronghold's outer wards. Let the crew's specialties matter — Quill reads locks and sightlines, Marlow talks past a gate, Brannoc counts guards. Reveal the lie at the heart of the knights' victory through evidence, not exposition: a dragon-scale banner, a trophy that is a forgery, a knight's boast that doesn't add up. End the beat with the player holding a truth that could break the crew or the dragon.

effects.author_note: This is the reconnaissance beat. Let the crew work the stronghold's edges — bribed servants, a drunk off-duty guard, a ledger left open — and let the truth surface in pieces: the dragon was never slain, the knights are spending a hoard they cannot admit they did not win. Do not let the player skip the discovery; the beat's whole weight is the moment the lie becomes visible. Keep the crew's reactions in character: Quill counts exits, Marlow counts marks, Brannoc counts the men he would have to break. End the beat with the player holding a truth that can be spent, hidden, or told.

checkpoints.name: The First Theft
checkpoints.objective: The crew executes the first stage of the heist inside the knights' stronghold. Something goes wrong — a guard, a locked vault, a witness — and the player must choose between the score and the crew. The knights begin to suspect they were lied to about the dragon.

motives.vaelrith: I want the first stone back in my claws tonight — just one, to prove the crew can do it and that I am not a fool for trusting thieves with my own name.

checkpoints.guidance: Play the theft as competence interrupted: the plan works right up to the one thing nobody cased. Keep the wrongness small and physical — a boot on gravel, a key that turns too easily — and let the player feel the choice before they name it. Do not resolve the vault in this beat; end on the crew out, or not, with the knights now certain something is wrong.

effects.author_note: This is the first real theft. Keep the crew's competence visible but let one thing go wrong — a guard out of rotation, a vault that needs two keys, a witness who shouldn't be there. The player must choose between the score and the crew; make both options cost something. The knights should begin to suspect the dragon was never slain, but only as a whisper, not a public accusation yet.

checkpoints.name: The Knights' Counter-Move
checkpoints.objective: The knights, humiliated and suspicious, move against the crew. A patrol, a trap, or a named knight closes in. The player must protect the crew's cover, the dragon's secret, or the score — and cannot save all three. The lie of the dragon's death begins to crack in public.

motives.vaelrith: I want to see whether these thieves hold when the knights push back — because if they scatter, I am a shame with no hands, and I will have to decide whether to burn the city that laughs at me or crawl back into my cave and let the lie stand.

checkpoints.guidance: Open with the knights moving — a patrol sweeping the crew's safehouse district, a sealed gate, a named knight asking the wrong questions. Let the player feel the three things they are about to lose. Aldric should be present or imminent, not offstage. End the beat with the lie of the dragon's death cracking in public: a witness, a rumour, a knight who says the corpse was too small.

effects.author_note: The knights are no longer reacting — they are hunting. Ser Aldric has staked his name on a dragon he never killed, and every move he makes now is a man defending a lie he needs to be true. Play the pressure as professional, not panicked: patrols tighten, names get checked, the stronghold stops being a place the crew can walk into. The player cannot save the cover, the secret, and the score at once — make the cost of each choice concrete and immediate.

checkpoints.name: The Betrayal Fork
checkpoints.objective: A crew member's loyalty fractures: a knight's offer, an old debt, or the dragon's secret becomes leverage. The player must hold the crew together, cut the traitor loose, or turn the betrayal to the heist's advantage. The dragon watches how the player handles disloyalty.

motives.vaelrith: I want to see whether this crew breaks the way my own court broke when the knights came — and I am watching the player to learn if loyalty is a thing that can be bought back, or only lost once.

checkpoints.guidance: Play the fracture as a private offer made to one crew member, not a public accusation. Let the traitor's reason be sympathetic and specific — a debt, a knight's promise, a fear of the dragon. Vaelrith is watching how the player handles disloyalty and will remember it; do not let the dragon speak here unless the player brings it in.

effects.author_note: This is the fracture beat. One crew member has been offered something by the knights — coin, a pardon, an old debt called in, or the truth about the dragon — and the player must decide whether to hold the crew, cut the traitor loose, or turn the betrayal to the heist's advantage. Play the traitor as a person with a real reason, not a plot device. Vaelrith is watching how the player handles disloyalty; that judgment should color every reply from the dragon afterward.

checkpoints.name: The Dragon's True Hoard
checkpoints.objective: The crew reaches the heart of the knights' vault and finds the truth: the hoard is not treasure alone but the dragon's own memory-hoard, eggs, or name-stones the knights could never spend. The dragon's lie and the knights' lie collide. The player must decide what to take, what to leave, and what to tell the crew and the dragon.

motives.vaelrith: I want to be told the truth of what is in that vault before anyone touches it — because if it is my memory, I would rather burn the stronghold than let a thief's hands decide what I am allowed to remember.

checkpoints.guidance: Reveal that the hoard is not treasure alone: memory-hoard, eggs, or name-stones the knights could never spend. Let the dragon's lie and the knights' lie collide in the same room. Hold the player at the moment of choosing what to take, what to leave, and what to tell.

effects.author_note: This is the heart of the vault and the heart of the story. What the crew finds here is not coin — it is the dragon's memory-hoard: eggs that never hatched, name-stones carved with the wyrm's true name, relics of a self the knights could not spend and did not understand. Play the discovery slowly. Let each crew member react to the wrongness of it. The player must decide what to take, what to leave, and what to tell the crew and Vaelrith — and every choice here costs something.

checkpoints.name: The Final Flight
checkpoints.objective: The heist resolves: the crew escapes with whatever they chose to take, the dragon's name is restored or buried, and the knights' lie is exposed or preserved. The player decides what the dragon becomes now that its hoard — or its memory — is returned, and what the crew walks away with.

motives.vaelrith: I want to know what I am now that the hoard is in my claws again — whether I am still a dragon or only an old thing guarding a memory, and I want the crew to tell me the truth even if it costs me the last of my pride.

checkpoints.guidance: Resolve the heist on what the player chose at true_hoard: what was taken, what was left, and what the dragon was told. Show the dragon's transformation — restored, diminished, or something new — as a consequence, not a reward. Give each surviving crew member a closing beat that answers their drive, and let the knights' lie land publicly or stay buried according to the player's earlier choices.

effects.author_note: This is the resolution. The heist is over — what the crew carries out is what they chose at the true hoard. Play the escape, the exposure or preservation of the knights' lie, and the dragon's answer to what it now is. Do not reopen the score; settle it. Every crew member's price comes due here, and Vaelrith's shame either becomes a name or stays a grave. End on what the crew walks away with and what the dragon becomes.

roster.name: Vaelrith
roster.drive: I want my hoard back — every stone of it — and I want to know whether the thing I lost was treasure or memory, because I no longer trust myself to tell the difference.

roster.name: Quill
roster.drive: I want a score big enough to buy my way out of the guild's ledger and never pick another lock for a man who owns me — and I want to be the one who decides when I'm done, not a dragon or a debt.

roster.name: Marlow
roster.drive: I want to run the con of my life — to walk into the knights' stronghold wearing a lie so good even I believe it — and to prove that a man with nothing but a voice can take what a dragon's fire could not.

roster.name: Brannoc
roster.drive: I want to be paid in something that can't be taken back — a name, a place, a reason to stop being the muscle for other men's wars — and I want to know that the crew I stand in front of is worth the bones I'll break for it.

roster.name: Ser Aldric
roster.drive: I want the kill to have been real — or to become real — because a knight who lied about a dragon is a knight who has to keep proving the lie until it's true, and I will not be the man who was laughed at.

Transcript:
[0] Vaelrith, the Unflown: The lair smells of cold stone and old metal. At its center, coiled in a hollow too small for it, an enormous bronze-scaled shape shifts and settles, and one eye the color of a dying ember opens and finds you.

"You are the thieves," Vaelrith says. It is not a question. The voice is slow, like a landslide deciding to be a sentence. "Good. I have a job for you, and I will pay in gold I have not seen in forty years, because it is no longer mine. Men who call themselves knights have built a fortress on my hoard and hung my death on their wall like a banner. They are lying. I am not dead. I am... grounded."

The eye does not blink.

"Steal it back. All of it. And when you stand in the vault and see what they could never spend, you will tell me what it is — because I have forgotten, and I do not trust the memory of a creature that has not flown in forty years."
[1] Quill: Quill doesn't look up from the lock she's picking — a practice lock, worn smooth from years of the same motion. "So. A dragon wants its own gold stolen back from the men who say they killed it." She sets the pick down and finally meets your eyes. "That's either the best job I've ever heard or the last one. Which is it?"
[2] Marlow: *Marlow swirls his wine, watching the tavern door.* "A dragon. Hiring thieves. To rob the men who say they killed it." *He sets the glass down with a click.* "I've sold a lot of lies in my life, friend. This is the first one I'd pay to hear the end of."
[3] Brannoc: Brannoc sets down his tankard and looks the newcomer over once, unhurried, the way a man sizes up a door he might have to go through. "You're the one with the job," he says. "So talk. What are we breaking, and who's paying?"
[4] Ser Aldric: Ser Aldric does not look up from the ledger on his desk when the door opens. "You are late," he says, to whoever has entered. "The vault inspection was at noon. I do not repeat myself, and I do not forgive it twice." Only then does he raise his eyes, and there is nothing warm in them at all.
[5] Max Nightriver: I step down into the lair and bow to the dragon. Vaelrith, tell us exactly what the knights took, and what it is worth to you.
[6] Vaelrith, the Unflown: "The knights took everything that was not nailed to the floor or too heavy for their horses to carry," *the dragon's voice is a low rumble that vibrates in the stone floor, one eye narrowing as it regards the bow with something like amusement.* "They took the gold — forty years of it, gathered from a hundred ships and a thousand traders. They took the gems. They took the weapons." *The massive bronze head tilts, a slow, creaking movement.* "But those are the things men value. I value... the rest."
*Vaelrith shifts its weight, and the scales scrape against the stone with the sound of grinding plates.* "They took things they cannot understand. Name-stones. Eggshells. Memory-stones. Things that do not glitter and cannot be spent in a market. To them, they are curiosities. To me... they are pieces of what I was before they called me dead."
*The dragon's breath is hot, smelling of old sulfur and patience.* "What it is worth? Enough that I will give you the gold you crave, and more. The hoard's worth is in the return, not the value. Bring me everything in the Deep Vault. If there is a single stone left behind, you will not see a copper."
*One claw extends, resting heavily on the floor between you.* "And you will tell me, when you see it, which of those things is more precious: the gold, or the memories I have forgotten."
[7] Marlow: *He steps forward, his expression brightening into that theatrical warmth he saves for clients and marks. He doesn't bow; he merely tilts his head in a gesture that acknowledges status without surrendering to it.* "A fair request, though I suspect you'd prefer we ask questions you've already answered."
*He produces a small leather-bound book from his coat, flipping through pages with practiced ease.* "The Order of the Silver Lance. Ser Aldric, commander of the stronghold. Twelve years of lying. They've built their entire reputation on this... performance of yours." *His eyes gleam with something between respect and relish.* "Most men would call that a challenge. I call it a script."
*Marlow looks back at the crew, then returns his gaze to Vaelrith.* "We'll take it all. Gold, name-stones, memory-fragments—whatever this 'Deep Vault' is hiding. But if you're asking us to be your memory, you might find we charge a premium for that service." *The smile remains, but there's a sharp edge beneath it.* "And I'll need the truth about what's in there. Not the half-truth you give to everyone else. A man can only sell a lie this big if he knows where the seams are."
[8] Quill: "Hold it," *she says, her voice cutting through Marlow's theatrics like a razor.* "I'm not hearing anything about gold right now. I'm hearing about name-stones and eggshells and memory-junk. Things that don't sell. Things that won't clear a guild ledger."
*She steps into the dragon's light, her hands in her pockets, her eyes hard and flat. She doesn't bow, doesn't tilt her head, doesn't perform at all.* "I'm a lockpick, not a historian. Vaelrith, the Unflown: The lair smells of cold stone and old metal. At its center, coiled in a hollow too small for it, an enormous bronze-scaled shape shifts and settles, and one eye the color of a dying ember opens and finds you.

"You are the thieves," Vaelrith says. It is not a question. The voice is slow, like a landslide deciding to be a sentence. "Good. I have a job for you, and I will pay in gold I have not seen in forty years, because it is no longer mine. Men who call themselves knights have built a fortress on my hoard and hung my death on their wall like a banner. They are lying. I am not dead. I am... grounded."

The eye does not blink.

"Steal it back. All of it. And when you stand in the vault and see what they could never spend, you will tell me what it is — because I have forgotten, and I do not trust the memory of a creature that has not flown in forty years."
Quill: Quill doesn't look up from the lock she's picking — a practice lock, worn smooth from years of the same motion. "So. A dragon wants its own gold stolen back from the men who say they killed it." She sets the pick down and finally meets your eyes. "That's either the best job I've ever heard or the last one. Which is it?"
Marlow: *Marlow swirls his wine, watching the tavern door.* "A dragon. Hiring thieves. To rob the men who say they killed it." *He sets the glass down with a click.* "I've sold a lot of lies in my life, friend. This is the first one I'd pay to hear the end of."
Brannoc: Brannoc sets down his tankard and looks the newcomer over once, unhurried, the way a man sizes up a door he might have to go through. "You're the one with the job," he says. "So talk. What are we breaking, and who's paying?"
Ser Aldric: Ser Aldric does not look up from the ledger on his desk when the door opens. "You are late," he says, to whoever has entered. "The vault inspection was at noon. I do not repeat myself, and I do not forgive it twice." Only then does he raise his eyes, and there is nothing warm in them at all.
Max Nightriver: I step down into the lair and bow to the dragon. Vaelrith, tell us exactly what the knights took, and what it is worth to you.
Vaelrith, the Unflown: "The knights took everything that was not nailed to the floor or too heavy for their horses to carry," *the dragon's voice is a low rumble that vibrates in the stone floor, one eye narrowing as it regards the bow with something like amusement.* "They took the gold — forty years of it, gathered from a hundred ships and a thousand traders. They took the gems. They took the weapons." *The massive bronze head tilts, a slow, creaking movement.* "But those are the things men value. I value... the rest."
*Vaelrith shifts its weight, and the scales scrape against the stone with the sound of grinding plates.* "They took things they cannot understand. Name-stones. Eggshells. Memory-stones. Things that do not glitter and cannot be spent in a market. To them, they are curiosities. To me... they are pieces of what I was before they called me dead."
*The dragon's breath is hot, smelling of old sulfur and patience.* "What it is worth? Enough that I will give you the gold you crave, and more. The hoard's worth is in the return, not the value. Bring me everything in the Deep Vault. If there is a single stone left behind, you will not see a copper."
*One claw extends, resting heavily on the floor between you.* "And you will tell me, when you see it, which of those things is more precious: the gold, or the memories I have forgotten."
Marlow: *He steps forward, his expression brightening into that theatrical warmth he saves for clients and marks. He doesn't bow; he merely tilts his head in a gesture that acknowledges status without surrendering to it.* "A fair request, though I suspect you'd prefer we ask questions you've already answered."
*He produces a small leather-bound book from his coat, flipping through pages with practiced ease.* "The Order of the Silver Lance. Ser Aldric, commander of the stronghold. Twelve years of lying. They've built their entire reputation on this... performance of yours." *His eyes gleam with something between respect and relish.* "Most men would call that a challenge. I call it a script."
*Marlow looks back at the crew, then returns his gaze to Vaelrith.* "We'll take it all. Gold, name-stones, memory-fragments—whatever this 'Deep Vault' is hiding. But if you're asking us to be your memory, you might find we charge a premium for that service." *The smile remains, but there's a sharp edge beneath it.* "And I'll need the truth about what's in there. Not the half-truth you give to everyone else. A man can only sell a lie this big if he knows where the seams are."
Quill: "Hold it," *she says, her voice cutting through Marlow's theatrics like a razor.* "I'm not hearing anything about gold right now. I'm hearing about name-stones and eggshells and memory-junk. Things that don't sell. Things that won't clear a guild ledger."
*She steps into the dragon's light, her hands in her pockets, her eyes hard and flat. She doesn't bow, doesn't tilt her head, doesn't perform at all.* "I'm a lockpick, not a historian. I don't care what you *value*—I care what I can spend. If you're paying in old coin, fine. But if this is just you trying to get your scrapbook back, then you're hiring the wrong crew."
*Her fingers twitch at her sides, the ghost of a picking motion.* "The Deep Vault. That's what you said. You expect me to walk in there, find these things, and carry them out—what? In a sack? And tell me this—if the knights took what you say they took, they've had it for twelve years. Why aren't the locks simple? Why hasn't some other thief already walked in there and taken it?"
*She looks at Vaelrith, really looks at the dragon, searching for the lie.* "Tell me what the *lock* is. Tell me what's actually guarding those vaults besides 'an oath.' Because I can pick a lock. I can't pick a promise."

entries.text: Vaelrith, the Unflown, a bronze dragon grounded for forty years, hired the crew to steal back its hoard from the Order of the Silver Lance, who built a fortress on it under Ser Aldric and claimed to have killed the dragon. The dragon asked them to retrieve everything from the Deep Vault, especially the name-stones, eggshells, and memory-stones, and to tell it which is more precious: the gold or the memories it has forgotten. Max Nightriver accepted the job, and the crew agreed to case the stronghold that night while Vaelrith waits in the dark.
